snippet.title: Thousands of Americans Celebrated a CEO Assassin | Ivy League Valedictorian | Luigi Mangione Case
snippet.description:
A man the entire country was hunting walked into a McDonald's in Pennsylvania, ordered food, and sat down to wait. Inside his backpack: a ghost gun, several fake IDs, thousands of dollars in cash, and a notebook investigators would later describe as a roadmap.

But the strangest part of this story is not how he was caught. It is who he was.

He was not a gang member. He was not a career criminal. He was an Ivy League computer scientist. A former valedictorian. The grandson of a wealthy real estate developer. A young man whose future seemed almost guaranteed.

And on December 4th, 2024, prosecutors say he walked up to Brian Thompson, the CEO of one of America's largest health insurance companies, and shot him outside a Manhattan hotel.

This is the story of Luigi Mangione. A case that raises a question America is still arguing about nearly two years later: how does someone with every advantage in life end up accused of one of the most shocking killings in modern memory? And why did thousands of people celebrate him after his arrest?

In this Vanto Crimes investigation:

The Manhattan shooting at the Hilton Hotel on the morning of UnitedHealthcare's investor conference.
The five-day manhunt across New York City and beyond.
The 911 call from an Altoona, Pennsylvania McDonald's that ended the search.
Inside the backpack: the ghost gun, the fake IDs, the cash, the notebook.
The three words allegedly written on the shell casings at the crime scene: DELAY. DENY. DEPOSE.
Luigi Mangione's Maryland upbringing, Ivy League education, and Penn valedictorian status.
The 2022 Hawaii surfing injury that may have changed everything.
The reading list and ideological shift in the months before the killing.
The summer 2024 disappearance, the missing persons report, and the months no one could find him.
The notebook entries prosecutors say prove premeditation, including the alleged line that named the target as "insurance."
Why federal prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.
And the central question: why did a young man who still had every option in life choose this one?

Luigi Mangione has pleaded not guilty to all federal and state charges. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Everything in this video that relates to alleged conduct is attributed to prosecutors, court filings, or law enforcement statements.

snippet.title: He Got Away for 40 Years, Then Someone in His Family Took a DNA Test | The Golden State Killer
snippet.description:
For more than forty years, the man who would later be called the Golden State Killer lived an ordinary life in California. He worked. He retired. He raised a family. His neighbours knew him. He was a former police officer. And he hid in plain sight while one of the longest manhunts in American history unfolded around him.

This is the full story of the Golden State Killer case, the original cold case that no one believed would ever be solved, the new forensic science that broke it open, and the single distant relative who, without knowing it, ended a 40-year investigation by uploading a DNA test online.

This case is a study in how forensic science changed forever. For decades, investigators believed that without the killer's own DNA on file, the case could never be solved. Then came consumer DNA testing. Millions of people across America voluntarily uploaded their genetic data to ancestry websites, looking for distant relatives and family history. They had no idea they were also building the largest investigative database in human history.

Investigators at the Sacramento County District Attorney's Office, working alongside a forensic genealogist, took a different approach. Instead of searching for the killer, they searched for someone related to the killer. The match they found was distant. A cousin. Someone who had never met the suspect. But it was enough. They built family trees backwards, sideways, and forwards, until one name emerged from the data: Joseph James DeAngelo. A former police officer. A grandfather. Living quietly in suburban California for decades.

On April 24, 2018, investigators arrested him outside his home. He pleaded guilty to thirteen counts of murder in June 2020 and is currently serving multiple life sentences without the possibility of parole.

This video does not glorify the crimes. It follows the investigation, the science, and the small details that finally connected a case that had been dead for forty years.

Sources include Sacramento County District Attorney's Office filings, FBI investigative records, court transcripts, and reporting from major outlets covering the case and the forensic genealogy methods that solved it.

snippet.title: Stanford Dropout Who Faked $9 Billion Company | Startup Fooled Silicon Valley | Theranos Case
snippet.description:
For nearly a decade, Elizabeth Holmes was hailed as the next Steve Jobs. A Stanford dropout at nineteen, she built Theranos into a company valued at nine billion dollars on the promise that a single drop of blood could replace hundreds of medical tests. She put former Secretaries of State on her board. She raised more than seven hundred million dollars from the most powerful investors in America. She put her devices inside Walgreens stores across Arizona and California.

There was just one problem. The machine she built never worked.

This is the full story of Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos, and one of the largest corporate frauds in Silicon Valley history. The story of the believers, the whistleblowers, the journalists, and the patients who paid the real price for a vision that was sold to the world before it ever existed.

For years, Theranos operated inside a culture that rewarded vision more than verification. The investors did not see the technology in action. The board did not ask if it worked. The employees who raised concerns were silenced, surveilled, or sued. And the patients who walked into a Walgreens trusting the system received results that, in many cases, were dangerously wrong.

The case unraveled in 2015 when Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyrou published an investigation showing that Theranos's flagship device, the Edison, did not perform as advertised. Federal regulators followed. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a notice declaring the company posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety. Theranos voided two years of patient results. The company collapsed.

The whistleblowers who made this possible were extraordinary. Erika Cheung, a twenty-two year old lab assistant straight out of college, saw outlier results being deleted instead of investigated. Tyler Shultz, the grandson of former Secretary of State and Theranos board member George Shultz, ran a proficiency test and watched the Edison return correct results on only twelve out of one hundred samples. Both reported what they saw. Both faced personal investigators, legal threats, and isolation. Tyler spent four hundred thousand dollars of his own money on legal fees defending himself from a company his grandfather had helped legitimize.

On January 3, 2022, Elizabeth Holmes was found guilty on four counts of fraud and conspiracy by a federal jury in San Jose. She was sentenced to eleven years and three months in federal prison. Her former partner and Theranos Chief Operating Officer, Ramesh Sunny Balwani, received twelve years and eleven months. Investors lost more than seven hundred million dollars. Patients across multiple states were left with results they could no longer trust.

This video follows the investigation, the evidence, the whistleblowers, and the cultural forces that allowed one young founder to fool an entire industry for more than a decade.

This video does not glorify Holmes or the events. It follows the timeline, the science, the testimony, and the small decisions that turned a stated mission to save lives into one of the most consequential corporate frauds in American history.

Holmes, CMS inspection records and notice of immediate jeopardy, congressional testimony, the published book Bad Blood by John Carreyrou, and contemporaneous reporting from Fortune, Forbes, and the New York Times.

snippet.description:
This is the story of the most expensive series of wrong decisions in the history of technology.

One company.

Three chances to win.

Three times they said no.

And lost everything.

This is Yahoo.

In the late 1990s Yahoo was the internet.

Not on the internet.

Not part of the internet.

Yahoo WAS the internet.

It was the homepage for hundreds of millions of people worldwide.

Its market cap hit $125 billion.

It was worth more than Boeing.

More than Merrill Lynch.

More than McDonald's.

The entire world passed through Yahoo every single day.

Then in 2002 they had the chance to buy Google.

Google was two guys and a search engine.

The asking price was $1 million.

Yahoo passed.

Let that sink in.

They passed on buying Google for $1 million.

Google is now worth $2 trillion.

Then in 2006 they had the chance to buy Facebook.

Mark Zuckerberg's board wanted to sell.

The price was $1 billion.

Zuckerberg pulled out at the last minute.

But Yahoo didn't fight for it.

Didn't push.

Didn't close the deal.

Facebook is now worth $1.4 trillion.

Then in 2008 Microsoft came to Yahoo with the most generous offer in tech history.

$44.6 billion.

A 62% premium above market price.

A lifeline handed to them on a silver platter.

CEO Jerry Yang turned it down.

Said Yahoo was worth more.

It was never worth more again.

What followed was a decade of slow painful decline.

Five CEOs in five years.

A $900 million acquisition of Tumblr.

Tumblr was later sold for $3 million.

A $1.1 billion acquisition of Tumblr creator Marissa Mayer's salary alone made headlines.

Nothing worked.

Nothing stuck.

Nothing saved them.

In 2017 Verizon bought Yahoo's entire core internet business for $4.8 billion.

The company that was worth $125 billion.

The company that could have bought Google for $1 million.

The company that turned down $44.6 billion from Microsoft.

Sold for $4.8 billion to a telephone company.

Yahoo had every single advantage.

First mover.

Brand recognition.

Hundreds of millions of users.

Billions in capital.

It lost to companies it could have bought for fractions of what it was worth.

The most valuable lesson in tech history — being first means absolutely nothing if you refuse to see what comes next.

snippet.title: Pizza Crust That Caught America's Most Hidden Serial Killer | The Gilgo Beach Case | Vanto Crimes
snippet.description:
For more than a decade, the killer of the Gilgo Four lived less than thirty minutes from where the bodies were found. He worked in Manhattan. He ran an architecture firm. He drove his children to school in Massapequa Park. And he hid in plain sight while a serial murder investigation unfolded around him.

This is the full story of the Gilgo Beach killings, the missed clues, the cold case years, the 2022 task force, and the small pieces of evidence that finally exposed Rex Heuermann.

This case is a study in how cold cases break open. A vehicle description sitting in a witness statement for years. Burner phone records that started overlapping with one specific neighbourhood. Cell tower pings inside a small area investigators came to call "the box." And a discarded pizza crust thrown into a Midtown Manhattan trash can that finally linked DNA evidence to the suspect.

By the time Rex Heuermann was arrested on July 14, 2023, the case had already touched four families for over a decade. By the time he pleaded guilty on April 8, 2026, the investigation had grown to include the murders of Maureen Brainard-Barnes, Melissa Barthelemy, Megan Waterman, Amber Lynn Costello, Jessica Taylor, Valerie Mack, Sandra Costilla, and Karen Vergata.

This video does not glorify the crimes. It follows the evidence, the investigation, and the small details that finally made the connections that mattered.

Sources include Suffolk County District Attorney's Office filings, court records, FBI reports, and reporting from The New York Times, Newsday, and other major outlets covering the case.

snippet.title: She Raised $900 Million With a Lie — And People Died Because of It 🩸💀
snippet.description:
Elizabeth Holmes was 19 years old when she dropped out of Stanford and told the world she was going to revolutionize medicine.

One drop of blood.
That's all it would take.
No needles. No labs. No waiting.
Just one tiny drop — and her machine would detect 200 diseases instantly.

Investors believed her.
Walgreens believed her.
Billionaires, generals, and government officials believed her.She raised $900 million.
Her company Theranos was valued at $9 billion.
She was on the cover of Fortune, Forbes, and Time magazine.
The world called her the next Steve Jobs.

There was just one problem.

The technology didn't work.

Not even close.

While patients were receiving cancer diagnoses, HIV results, and life-changing medical decisions — every single result was being generated by conventional Siemens machines hidden in the back of the lab.

Theranos was faking everything.

When a Wall Street Journal reporter started asking questions, Holmes went on television and called it a smear campaign.

She threatened sources with lawyers.
She silenced employees with NDAs.
She kept going — for years.

Then the regulators came.
The lab was shut down.
The indictment followed.
In 2022 Elizabeth Holmes was convicted on four counts of fraud.
Sentenced to 11 years in prison.

But the victims weren't just investors who lost money.
Cancer patients missed real diagnoses.
HIV patients received false positives.
Doctors made treatment decisions based on numbers that were completely fabricated.

Real people. Real consequences. Real harm.

This is the story of the most dangerous startup in Silicon Valley history — and what happens when fake it till you make it collides with actual human lives.
